Iranian authorities have released footage purporting to show the launch of missiles and drones aimed at U.S. forces stationed at the King Hussein and Al-Azraq air bases in Jordan.
Tehran characterized the operation as a direct response to a U.S. strike against Iranian military positions on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
While Iranian state media claimed the barrage caused severe damage to key infrastructure, regional military authorities reported that defensive systems successfully intercepted most of the incoming projectiles.
The exchange marks a significant escalation, heightening security concerns and driving volatility across global oil markets.
Watch this video from Reuters. 
Also Read:

Iran said Monday it struck U.S. military bases in Jordan in retaliation for an American attack on Larak Island near the Strait of Hormuz after Washington said it acted to stop Iranian forces from laying sea mines. A U.S. official confirmed Iran launched several ballistic missiles at an American base in Jordan but said none struck U.S. facilities and there were no reports of damage or casualties.
Jordan’s military said its air defenses intercepted eight missiles fired from Iran. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said U.S. bases in Jordan had been used to support the strike on Larak Island, which Tehran said killed and wounded Iranian military personnel and civilians. Tehran warned it would respond “decisively” to any further U.S. military action and blamed Washington and countries supporting it for any escalation.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) eased its airspace warnings for Jordan and Lebanon on August 31, 2026, the same day Jordan’s military said it had intercepted eight missiles over the kingdom at dawn.
The agency revised its Conflict Zone Information Bulletin (CZIB) for Jordan, dropping the recommendation that operators avoid the Amman flight information region (FIR) altogether. The previous version prohibited airlines from operating in the Amman FIR at any altitude or flight level.
The revised bulletin asks operators to take potential risks into account, maintain up-to-date risk assessments and contingency plans, and remain prepared to follow instructions from state authorities at short notice. EASA assessed the risk to civil flights as medium rather than high and extended the bulletin’s validity to September 30, 2026.
EASA attributed the change to a quiet August 2026. After a sustained increase in kinetic military activity in July 2026, no kinetic activity was observed in August 2026, the bulletin states. It also notes that Jordanian authorities have published no conflict-related airspace restrictions or route closures, meaning operators should be prepared for tactical deconfliction if activity resumes.
The same day, the official spokesman for the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement carried by the state news agency Petra that air defense systems intercepted eight missiles that penetrated the kingdom’s airspace at dawn on August 31, 2026. He said the missiles were destroyed before they posed a threat to citizens or property.
EASA restores limited access to Beirut
EASA also revised its Lebanon bulletin, restoring an exception for Beirut Rafic Hariri International Airport (BEY). Operators may fly to and from Beirut where the approach begins over the sea, and the departure ends over the sea, subject to an up-to-date risk assessment and continuous risk monitoring.
Lebanese airspace remains assessed as high risk outside that carve-out. EASA said recurrent ceasefire violations were observed in August 2026, primarily in southern Lebanon.
UAE reports drone approaching from Iran
Separately, the UAE Ministry of Defense said on August 31, 2026, that the UAE Air Force engaged a drone detected over the country’s territorial waters as it approached from Iran, in a statement carried by the state news agency WAM.
EASA told airlines to avoid Gulf airspace covering Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates on July 14, 2026.
Both revised bulletins remain valid until September 30, 2026, unless reviewed earlier. CZIBs are recommendations. They apply to operators governed by Commission Regulation (EU) 965/2012 and to third-country operators holding EASA authorizations, while national authorities retain control over their own airspace.

Iran says two killed in US strikes on island in Strait of Hormuz
In short:
A US attack on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz killed two people and injured several others, Iranian state media reported.
US President Donald Trump had earlier posted about strikes on another Iranian island, a move JD Vance says was about "sending a message".
It comes as the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters, an attack that followed the United States and Iran exchanging fire over the weekend.
The US attack on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz killed two people and injured several others, Iranian state media has reported.
It came as Donald Trump used a social media post to threaten to blow Iran's Kharg Island to "smithereens", a post vice-president JD Vance would later say was "sending a message".
Iran's official IRNA news agency, quoting Hossein Amir Teymouri, the governor of nearby Qeshm Island, said on Monday that two were killed in strikes on Larak Island late on Sunday.
"The injured in the incident are receiving medical services and their treatment is ongoing," it added, without specifying whether the victims were soldiers or civilians.
It comes as the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters, an attack that followed the United States and Iran exchanging fire over the weekend — the first time in a month.
During the lull in fighting, the US has been ratcheting up economic pressure on Iran with the hope of forcing concessions out of Tehran, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping.
In his latest attempt to push Iran towards a deal, Mr Trump's Truth Social account on Sunday posted an AI-generated video of missiles hitting Kharg Island alongside the message: "Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!"
A US official said on Monday the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes, while an Iranian official dismissed Trump's post as "laughable".
Defending the post, Mr Vance said it was evidence the US president "likes to switch it up on social media a little bit".
"He would be the first to say he doesn't make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he's sending a message to the Iranians," he said after being asked about Mr Trump's post.
After the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, Iran established a chokehold on the vital strait, though which a fifth of the world's traded oil passed in peacetime, slowing ship traffic to a trickle.
That has roiled the global economy, raising prices worldwide for energy and other goods.
As the fighting resumed, the price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed above $US90, up about 25 per cent from the start of the war, presenting a growing problem for US President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted US military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began.
UAE says Iranian attack is a 'dangerous escalation'
In a short statement, the UAE Defense Ministry said it "dealt with" an Iranian drone that was detected over its waters approaching from Iran.
There were no reports of damage.
"This dangerous escalation constitutes a blatant violation of the UAE's sovereignty, security and stability, and a direct threat to the safety of its citizens and residents," the Foreign Ministry said.
The Defense Ministry later issued a second statement denying a claim by the Iranian army that the Al Minhad Air Base in Dubai had been targeted, saying it was false.
In the wake of the US attack on Sunday, Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Monday that Iran would "not hesitate to exercise the inherent right of legitimate defense and will respond decisively to any military aggression."
Iran says it has right to defend itself
Before heading to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization's summit in Kyrgyzstan with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who has favoured a negotiated end to the conflict, stressed Iran was not seeking war.
"But," he said, "we will respond decisively to aggressors."
The summit brings together a group billed as a counterweight to US global influence, and includes Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Mr Pezeshkian was scheduled to meet with Mr Putin on the sidelines on Tuesday.
Attack comes after weeks of rising economic pressure
Meantime, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was set to host meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in North Carolina on Monday and Tuesday, which come as Washington pressures other countries to help the US economically isolate Iran.
The shifting strategy centres on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran.
Two weeks ago, the UAE suspended all trade with Iran after saying it had come under renewed fire from Iran with two missiles fired at shipping traffic splashing down harmlessly in the Persian Gulf.
Iran denied the attack.
Mr Bessent later suggested it was pressure from Washington that led to the UAE decision.
Mr Trump stressed last week that he was "not in a hurry" to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he has continued making the case that the Islamic Republic's leadership is on the ropes.
Appointments to Iran's senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signalled Tehran's defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home.
US military says strike on Iranian rocket launchers 'limited' and 'precise'
On Sunday, US Central Command said it had struck Iranian launchers after observing forces with Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military said last week it had completed clearing sea mines from the waterway's international shipping routes.
US military officials disputed Iran's claim the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a "limited, precise action" against what they said were mine-laying forces.
Iranian state television later showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired at American bases in Jordan, and Jordan's military said it intercepted eight that had entered its airspace.
The last time the US military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, when it announced a "heavy wave of strikes" on dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets including coastal surveillance and defence sites.
